paper.title: ProgressNet: Sketching and Prompting with a Frozen Text-to-Image Model
paper.abstract: Abstract Humans draw progressively: a few strokes, a look at the result, a stroke erased, a prompt revised. Image generators do not work this way. They typically take a finished sketch and produce the image in a single pass, so every edit starts the picture again, and the models that do keep state across turns are driven by text, cannot take a stroke, and are too slow to draw with. We present ProgressNet , a training-free framework that lets a frozen text-to-image model follow a drawing session as it unfolds: strokes are added and erased, the prompt is revised, and the image keeps up at about a second per turn. It needs no new parameters because the frozen model already has what a progressive generator needs, a pathway through which the previous turn can be remembered, layers that can carry appearance forward without freezing structure, and an internal signal of how far to trust an unfinished sketch; three inference-time mechanisms ( Previous-Concept Memory , Layer-Selective K/V Injection and Banded Adaptive Control ) use each in turn. As a sketch fills in, every existing method degrades, the FID of the FLUX+ControlNet baseline doubling between 10% and 100% completion on FS-COCO, while ProgressNet’s barely moves; it maintains strong fidelity and progressive coherence across three sketch domains and is preferred by users over five competitors, most widely on erasure.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Humans are visual creatures. We drew before we wrote, and drawing remains the most natural way to think through a visual idea and share it. Generative AI has opened a remarkable channel for this: a sentence now produces a picture ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ) , in well under a second with few-step distillation ( Luo et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2023 ) , and because a sentence is a poor description of a picture, control has steadily grown beyond text, to edges, depth and layout ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Mou et al., 2024 ) , to reference images ( Ye et al., 2023 ; Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ) , and most recently to a sketch drawn beside the prompt box ( OpenAI, 2026 ) . Sketch is the natural end of that road: it is how people convey shape and intent when words run out ( Eitz et al., 2012 ; Koley et al., 2024 ) . Yet every one of these systems takes the sketch as a finished input and produces the image in a single pass, and nobody draws that way. A drawing is made over time: a few strokes, a look, a stroke erased, a line redrawn, often a change of mind about what the picture is of ( Fig. 1 ). What a person needs is not a picture from a sketch but a picture that keeps up with the sketching: one that follows each added stroke, lets go of each erased one, absorbs a revised prompt, leaves everything else untouched, and answers fast enough to feel like a response rather than a resubmission. This paper is about that interaction. ProgressNet lets a frozen text-to-image model support all of it, drawing, erasing and prompt revision, at about a second per turn and with no training. Figure 2: Flux+ControlNet imprints raw stroke edges and visually drifts across progressive turns; ours adapts smoothly while maintaining temporal coherence. To the best of our knowledge, no existing system does all. Sketch-conditioned generation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Koley et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) is stateless: each turn regenerates the scene from nothing, so appearance drifts with every stroke and an erased stroke leaves a ghost, because nothing withdraws the evidence it added ( Fig. 2 ). Interactive sketch systems lower the cost of regeneration without removing its statelessness ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2024 ) , and Subjective Camera ( Chen et al., 2025b ) follows a drawing order by latent optimisation that takes minutes per scene. Image editing models ( Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) do handle turn-by-turn interaction, but for a different kind of turn: the image enters as a second token stream in joint attention and the change is given in words, so there is no pathway for a stroke map and no way to say that a stroke is gone, and tens of denoising steps over a doubled sequence make each turn take seconds rather than the fraction of a second a drawing person will wait. ProgressNet therefore builds on the architecture that accepts strokes, a frozen flow-matching backbone with a ControlNet, and stays in the few-step regime that makes interaction possible. Following a drawing session with a frozen model raises three problems, and each has a simple answer inside the model. Remembering. The model must remember what it generated last turn. The ControlNet’s tile branch accepts an RGB image, so the previous output can be fed back as an explicit appearance memory, and because that memory lives in pixel space the user’s operations map onto it directly: an added stroke keeps it, an erased stroke white-fills its region, a new prompt relaxes the regions the user has not committed to ( Previous-Concept Memory , PCM; Section 4.1 ). Carrying forward. The model must carry that memory without freezing what should change. Training-free editors inject cached attention at the layers most vital to forming the image ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) ; under progression those are exactly the layers that must absorb new strokes, and locking them yields images that stop responding as the drawing grows. Injecting at the least vital layers instead keeps appearance while structure stays free ( Layer-Selective K/V Injection , LS-KVI; Section 4.2 ). Trusting the sketch. The model must balance adherence to an unfinished sketch with preservation of previous appearance. We regulate this balance indirectly, using changes in cached ControlNet memory features between the two preceding completed turns to modulate memory strength across layer bands and solver steps, while structural control remains fixed (Banded Adaptive Control, BAC; Section 4.3 ). Together the three add 0.068 0.068 s to a two-step FLUX generation. The result is a generator whose quality does not decay as the drawing fills in: on FS-COCO ( Chowdhury et al., 2022 ) the FID of FLUX+ControlNet doubles between 10% and 100% completion and every baseline degrades the same way, while ProgressNet’s moves by under one point. Because frame-to-frame similarity alone rewards a method that ignores the new stroke, we introduce a progressive fidelity-coherence score (PFC) combining temporal coherence with completion-level distributional quality. Our contributions are (i) the first training-free system for progressive generation from sketch and text that supports stroke addition, erasure and prompt revision at interactive rates; (ii) PCM, LS-KVI and BAC, with the findings that vital-layer injection over-locks under progression and that inter-turn ControlNet feature redistribution is a usable online control signal, validated across two backbones and four sketch domains; (iii) a protocol and score for progressive generation, with results on three sketch domains and user study in which ProgressNet is preferred over five competitors, most widely on erasure. None of the three mechanisms is sketch-specific.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Controllable image generation spans ControlNet-style residual conditioning ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , multi-condition control ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , lightweight adapters ( Mou et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2023 ) , layout grounding ( Li et al., 2023b ; Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ) , and training-free feature steering ( Mo et al., 2024 ; Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) , recently ported to DiT and rectified-flow backbones ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Tan et al., 2025 ) . Inversion-based editing ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) , attention injection ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) , and few-step distillation ( Song et al., 2024 ; Sauer et al., 2023 ) improve editability and latency, bringing sketch interaction near real time ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ) . Others mitigate text-sketch conflict by re-weighting cross-attention ( Chefer et al., 2023 ; Phung et al., 2024 ) or rescaling the control residual ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Cohen et al., 2025 ) . All operate single-shot: none tracks how sketch–text conflict evolves across turns, nor preserves prior content as the condition changes. ProgressNet targets this non-stationary setting via training-free temporal memory, selective feature reuse, and ControlNet-driven adaptive control, detailed in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: ProgressNet builds on flow-matching backbones ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2025 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) with Union ControlNet. Joint attention over latent and context tokens exposes the K/V features later reused by LS-KVI ( Section 4.2 ), while spatial conditions such as Canny edges and tile memory are introduced through ControlNet residuals, 𝐡 ′ = 𝐡 + λ ​ 𝐫 \mathbf{h}^{\prime}=\mathbf{h}+\lambda\mathbf{r} . This formulation also makes the control strength λ \lambda a critical factor under few-step inference, where over- or under-conditioning cannot be corrected over many denoising steps ( Section 4.3 ). Our pilot studies ( Figs. 3a and 3b ) show that existing formulations struggle to maintain a coherent progressive state: appearance can drift between turns, a fixed control strength can either imprint partial strokes too strongly or under-enforce them, and erased content may persist when the sketch is revised. ProgressNet addresses these coupled failures through explicit concept memory, selective temporal feature reuse, and adaptive control modulation. (a) Progressive sketching. (b) Stroke removal and re-addition. Figure 3: Pilot studies illustrating failure modes of existing methods: temporal drift, prompt-sketch conflict under partial strokes, and contradiction upon stroke removal. (a) Under progressive sketching, FLUX+ControlNet and StableFlow show temporal instability and artifacts on the partial strokes ( red borders), while ours remains stable across turns. (b) When strokes are removed and re-added (Seq. 1-3), FLUX+ControlNet fails to preserve established concepts, shifting identity across turns.

sections.heading: 4 Proposed Methodology
sections.text: Overview. Given a sketch 𝐒 t \mathbf{S}_{t} , prompt P t P_{t} , and previous output I t − 1 I_{t-1} , we generate I t = 𝒢 ⁡ ( 𝐒 t , P t , I t − 1 , θ ) I_{t}=\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{S}_{t},P_{t},I_{t-1};\theta) while keeping pretrained weights θ \theta frozen and supporting stroke addition, removal, and prompt updates. ProgressNet combines three mechanisms: (i) PCM uses operation-aware tile conditioning to preserve prior appearance ( Section 4.1 ); (ii) LS-KVI reuses previous-turn features only at selected layers to maintain context while permitting structural change ( Section 4.2 ); and (iii) BAC applies retrospective, step- and band-specific modulation to the memory-conditioning ControlNet stream using cached inter-turn comparisons.

Since the memory is an RGB image, it can be edited directly according to the user operation before conditioning, with no extra learned module or additional learned preprocessing. PCM thus turns a stateless sketch-conditioned generator into an operation-aware progressive one, entirely at inference time.

sections.heading: 4.2 Layer-Selective K/V Injection (LS-KVI)
sections.text: PCM anchors successive generations via memory conditioning, but internal representations can still drift as attention is recomputed at each step. Training-free editors reduce such drift by reusing attention features, either injecting source features into key DiT layers ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) or reusing layer-specific K/V features ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Dalva et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . However, they target prompt-only editing, not the control-driven edits central to progressive drawing. Figure 5: Vital vs. non-vital layer. Vital-layer injection locks in early details, losing adaptability, while non-vital LS-KVI preserves appearance and sharpness as structure follows sketch. From image editing to progressive control. Progressive generation differs from text-guided editing. In editing, feature injection preserves a source image while text updates selected semantics. In progressive control, each turn adds a new spatial signal via ControlNet, and new strokes may change geometry, pose, or even the concept. Carrying strong previous-turn features through influential layers can thus conflict with the current structure and over-preserve content that should evolve, as we observe when adapting vital-layer injection to progressive sketching ( Fig. 5 ). This suggests a different principle: progressive generation should not freeze the layers most responsible for forming the current concept. We therefore leave vital layers without direct temporal K/V injection and reuse features at selected lower-vitality layers, assessing the resulting preservation and adaptation empirically. Progressive layer selection. Following the residual-bypass analysis used to study layer importance ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) , we measure layer vitality directly under progressive controlled generation rather than prompt-only editing. For each transformer layer ℓ \ell , we bypass that layer through its residual connection and measure the output change across progressive sketch stages. Neither, however, determines how strongly the preceding memory should constrain generation with progressive drawing. We address this through adaptive memory control in Section 4.3 .

sections.heading: 4.3 Banded Adaptive Control (BAC)
sections.text: PCM and LS-KVI preserve information across turns, but PCM retains a fixed memory-control strength. Rather than learning a mixing policy or modifying conditioning flow ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Cohen et al., 2025 ) , we ask whether the pretrained model itself reveals how its control response changes under progressive updates. Control is band- and step-asymmetric. We first study how ControlNet changes the backbone during progressive generation. We evaluate generation quality at specific sketch-completion stages (Table 1 ) and progressive stability across representative transitions (Table 2 ), while preserving stroke order and captions. We measure distributional quality with FID-I ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and FID-C ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2023 ) , semantic fidelity with DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , and text alignment with CLIPScore ( Hessel et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ) and T5-Cos (BLIP-2 captions ( Li et al., 2023a ) + T5 embeddings ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) ). For progression, PFC-DINO and PFC-LPIPS measure temporal stability. We additionally report quality-adjusted cross-completion robustness in distributional (Dist.), visual (Vis.), textual (Text), and overall dimensions, normalized to the FLUX baseline ( 100 100 ). Full definitions are provided in Appendix A.2 .

sections.heading: 5.1 Quantitative Results
sections.text: We compare against Sketch-a-Sketch (S-a-S) ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ) , SDXS ( Song et al., 2024 ) , Conditional Balance (CB) ( Cohen et al., 2025 ) , FLUX+ControlNet ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and StableFlow (SF) ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) . Table 1 evaluates generation quality at 10%, 50%, 100% sketch completion across three sketch datasets. ProgressNet maintains strong semantic fidelity: DINOv2 is highest or tied-highest at nearly all completion levels, with competitive CLIP/T5 alignment. This suggests the method stays faithful to the target image and prompt throughout the drawing, rather than only at the final drawing state. Table 2 presents progressive fidelity and inter-turn coherence using PFC-DINO and PFC-LPIPS, which assess coherence while also accounting for quality. ProgressNet obtains the highest mean PFC-DINO/PFC-LPIPS on FS-COCO and Sketchy, and the highest final-transition scores across all three sketch domains. The cross-completion indices additionally summarize quality and its variation across completion levels. Figure 7: Progressive sketching (left) and sketch removal (right). Competing methods frequently drift or introduce structural artifacts as strokes evolve, while ProgressNet preserves appearance and scene consistency while adapting to added or removed strokes. Figure 8: Qualitative results. Top-left : Cross-method comparison on progressive giraffe and zebra sketching; red circles indicate temporal drift and artifacts, while ours remains coherent. Bottom-left : Creative comparison with Nano Banana Pro, where ours better preserves the evolving sketch structure and intended concept. Right : Fine-grained progressive edits to the giraffe ear, mane, and scenery; ours performs localized adaptation while maintaining global consistency.

sections.heading: 5.2 Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figs. 8 and 8 examine how progressive memory supports generation as the sketch is continuously extended, revised, or locally edited. In Fig. 8 , comparisons against standard baselines show that ProgressNet better preserves appearance and scene context during progressive sketching and remains coherent when previously drawn strokes are removed. Fig. 8 extends this evaluation to cross-method comparisons and more demanding interactions against Nano Banana Pro, including fine-grained giraffe and scene-level edits as well as open-ended creative generation. These examples also show reduced temporal drift and stroke-induced artifacts under progressive updates. Across these cases, the progressive sketching process allows local structure to evolve without repeatedly reinterpreting the established image, while the retained visual state provides an important basis for subsequent edits. Together, these illustrate the practical benefit of progressive memory: users can incrementally develop, revise, and refine an image while preserving the context established earlier.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We proposed ProgressNet, a training-free framework for progressive generation that stabilizes interactions between evolving strokes and prompts. PCM and LS-KVI preserve temporal consistency, while BAC uses retrospective memory-feature divergence to adapt memory. ProgressNet enables progressive drawing by improving fidelity and alignment across completion levels with near-real-time performance. Our work opens avenues for more modality-agnostic progressive generation. Limitations. (i) ProgressNet is primarily evaluated with sketch-based control; extending its memory and adaptive-control mechanisms to other modalities, such as depth and pose, remains unexplored. (ii) BAC uses predefined layer bands and modulation bounds; automatically identifying control-sensitive regions on different conditioning modalities is a promising future direction.

sections.heading: A.1 Dataset and Progressive Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We evaluate three complementary sketch domains using fixed evaluation subsets and identical inputs for every compared method. sections.heading: A.4 Interpreting the Ablation Progression
sections.text: FID-I and FID-C measure distributional quality in Inception and CLIP image-feature spaces, respectively; DINOv2 measures paired visual-semantic fidelity, while CLIPScore and T5-Cos assess text alignment. We therefore interpret temporal and fidelity metrics jointly, complemented by qualitative and operation-level evaluations. From 30% completion onward on FS-COCO, the full system (PCM + LS-KVI + BAC) obtains the strongest FID-C and remains at or above the other ablation variants on CLIPScore and T5-Cos across the reported stages ( Tables 7 and 4 ). Its FID-C remains low and stable across 30–100% completion (0.144, 0.141, 0.142, 0.141, 0.143), while CLIPScore and T5-Cos remain competitive throughout. Together, the full system maintains strong FID-I while improving FID-C and textual alignment across later completion stages; the qualitative BAC analysis separately examines difficult sketch–prompt configurations.

sections.heading: Inference configuration.
sections.text: All ProgressNet experiments use FLUX.1-schnell with Union ControlNet at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution. Unless otherwise stated, the structural and memory-conditioning scales are fixed to λ s = 0.5 \lambda_{s}=0.5 and λ m = 0.65 \lambda_{m}=0.65 , respectively. Live progressive generation uses two inference steps in bfloat16 on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU.

sections.heading: Sketch preprocessing.
sections.text: The line-based sketch condition is converted to a binary structural map before being resized to the 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 ControlNet input resolution. We convert the sketch to grayscale, threshold it at intensity 200 200 , invert the binary map so that drawn strokes form the active condition, and resize using nearest-neighbour interpolation. Figure 10: Extended qualitative comparison of vital-layer vs. non-vital-layer K/V injection across four FS-COCO samples at progressive sketch completions ( 20 % 20\% , 50 % 50\% , 80 % 80\% , 100 % 100\% ). Vital-layer ( ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) ) injection progressively corrupts appearance, shifting illumination (clock tower darkens), altering identity (horse rider changes clothing and pose), and inducing color drift (banana flower saturates), while non-vital-layer ( { 5 , 6 , 7 , 10 , 13 , 14 } \{5,6,7,10,13,14\} ) injection preserves consistent appearance, lighting, and identity throughout the progression. This extends the single-sample comparison in Fig. 5 of the main paper.

sections.heading: B.1 Previous-Concept Memory implementation
sections.text: PCM derives its commitment mask C t C_{t} from the processed current sketch. We combine a dilated stroke-proximity support with flood-filled enclosed regions; the resulting mask marks content that should remain committed under subsequent interaction. At the two extremes, C t = 1 C_{t}{=}1 denotes fully committed content retained from I t − 1 I_{t-1} , whereas C t = 0 C_{t}{=}0 denotes fully relaxed regions during a prompt update; intermediate values provide a soft blend between the previous output and the neutral prior. For stroke addition, the previous output is used unchanged as memory. For stroke removal, evidence inside the erased region is withdrawn by neutral white filling before tile conditioning. For prompt updates, committed content is preserved while uncommitted regions are replaced by the neutral gray prior, as defined in Eq. 1 of the main paper. The same mask construction is used for all datasets and all interaction sequences.

sections.heading: Commitment-mask construction.
sections.text: The soft commitment mask combines two complementary supports. For stroke-proximity support, pixels with grayscale intensity below 200 200 are treated as sketch pixels, dilated by 24 24 pixels using an elliptical kernel, and Gaussian-smoothed with a 41 × 41 41\times 41 kernel. For enclosed regions, we first morphologically close sketch gaps using a 17 × 17 17\times 17 elliptical kernel, corresponding to an 8 8 -pixel closing radius. We then flood-fill the exterior from the image boundary and retain the non-exterior region as the enclosed support, followed by Gaussian smoothing with a 21 × 21 21\times 21 kernel. The final commitment mask is the pixelwise maximum of the proximity and enclosed-region supports and is clipped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . These parameters are held fixed throughout all reported experiments.

sections.heading: B.2 Choice of vital and non-vital layers
sections.text: The mechanism is made visible in Fig. 10 , which extends the single-sample comparison of Fig. 5 across four diverse FS-COCO scenes. In each case, vital-layer injection progressively overrides appearance attributes that should remain stable: the clock tower’s warm sunset illumination darkens into an unnatural palette; the horse rider’s clothing, skin tone, and pose drift across completions; and the banana flower saturates in color as strokes accumulate. In contrast, non-vital-layer injection (bottom rows) maintains consistent lighting, identity, and color across the four examples. Empirically, injecting at these lower-vitality layers preserves appearance more effectively while allowing structural adaptation. The giraffe retains its pose and forest backdrop; the clock tower preserves warm tones and adapts precise details correctly; the horse rider maintains consistent attire and posture; and the banana flower evolves structurally without color shift. This is precisely the property exploited by LS-KVI under progression: temporal smoothing at layers whose individual absence leaves generation quality intact ( Section 4.2 , main paper), enabling the concept to structurally evolve with new strokes while preserving what the image was . We therefore inject at non-vital layers throughout. Under the FLUX vitality analysis, the six lowest-vitality layers selected for injection are { 5 , 6 , 7 , 10 , 13 , 14 } \{5,6,7,10,13,14\} , with α kv = 0.3 \alpha_{\mathrm{kv}}{=}0.3 in all reported experiments. The cache is refreshed after each generation and cleared on stroke removal so that correspondence pathways associated with erased content are not reintroduced.

sections.heading: K/V tensor and cache implementation.
sections.text: LS-KVI attaches forward hooks to the key and value projections of joint attention at the selected transformer blocks. The full projected key and value tensors are retained rather than spatially or channel-wise subsampled. For a selected layer ℓ \ell , the current turn uses 𝐊 ℓ ′ t = 𝐊 ℓ t + α kv ​ 𝐊 ℓ t − 1 , 𝐕 ℓ ′ t = 𝐕 ℓ t + α kv ​ 𝐕 ℓ t − 1 , \mathbf{K}^{\prime t}_{\ell}=\mathbf{K}^{t}_{\ell}+\alpha_{\mathrm{kv}}\mathbf{K}^{t-1}_{\ell},\qquad\mathbf{V}^{\prime t}_{\ell}=\mathbf{V}^{t}_{\ell}+\alpha_{\mathrm{kv}}\mathbf{V}^{t-1}_{\ell}, with α kv = 0.3 \alpha_{\mathrm{kv}}=0.3 . During generation, the current projection outputs are captured for the next turn; after the generation finishes, the captured tensors are committed as the new reference cache. The cache is indexed by transformer layer and is refreshed after every completed turn. On stroke removal, the cached K/V state is cleared before the subsequent generation so that features associated with erased content cannot be re-injected.

sections.heading: Layer-selection protocol.
sections.text: The injection subset is selected once using the residual-bypass vitality analysis described in Section 4.2 : each candidate transformer layer is bypassed individually over progressive sketch stages and ranked by the resulting output deviation. LS-KVI uses the lowest-vitality layers and keeps this subset and α kv = 0.3 \alpha_{\mathrm{kv}}=0.3 fixed across the reported datasets rather than re-selecting layers per dataset. sections.heading: Erasure-specific LS-KVI state invalidation.
sections.text: We quantitatively evaluate stroke removal on 100 FS-COCO sequences using a controlled S 50 → S 70 → S 50 S_{50}\!\rightarrow\!S_{70}\!\rightarrow\!S_{50} add–erase cycle, where the final sketch is identical to the initial 50 % 50\% state. All generation settings and preceding history are fixed; we vary only whether the previous LS-KVI cache is retained or invalidated during removal. Return LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) measure recovery toward the original I 50 I_{50} output, while Recovery denotes the LPIPS improvement relative to the preceding I 50 → I 70 I_{50}\!\rightarrow\!I_{70} change. We additionally report error inside the erased region and appearance change outside it. Invalidating stale LS-KVI state reduces return LPIPS by 30.9 % 30.9\% and improves recovery in 93 / 100 93/100 sequences (paired Wilcoxon p = 7.1 × 10 − 15 p=7.1{\times}10^{-15} ). It also reduces erased-region error in 91 / 100 91/100 cases, showing that stale temporal correspondences can resist destructive updates.

sections.heading: Appendix D User Study Details
sections.text: We recruited participants from open communities through an online Gradio interface. Both studies were conducted double-blind: method identities were hidden, presentation order was randomized per trial, and participants were not told which system produced an output.

sections.heading: Study 1: overall generation quality.
sections.text: Participants evaluated six methods (Ours, Flux+ControlNet ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ) , SDXS ( Song et al., 2024 ) , Sketch-a-Sketch ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ) , StableFlow ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) , and Conditional Balance ( Cohen et al., 2025 ) ) across 10 diverse samples. For each sample, participants (i) ranked the six methods by overall visual preference, (ii) rated temporal coherency using a continuous 0–1 slider while viewing progressive-generation videos, and (iii) rated generation quality on a five-point Likert scale from Very Poor to Excellent. These correspond to the Pref. , Coher. , and Qual. columns in Table 3 . The reported values aggregate responses across participants and evaluated samples and are presented as normalized criterion-wise scores, with higher values indicating stronger user preference.

sections.heading: Study 2: operation-level capabilities.
sections.text: Participants first selected the better output for 12 erasure samples and three editing-pipeline samples, evaluating stroke-removal and sketch-modification fidelity. They then viewed side-by-side videos of complete progressive sessions and judged prompt-guided progression, fine-grained drawing quality, fine-grained erasure quality, and content preservation across edits. These map to the Erase , Edit , Prog. , F-Draw , F-Erase , and Preserv. columns in Table 3 . As in Study 1, responses are aggregated across participants and evaluated samples and reported as normalized criterion-wise scores, with higher values indicating stronger outcomes. Scores are normalized independently within each criterion across methods.

sections.heading: Controllable Image Generation.
sections.text: ControlNet ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) established spatial conditioning through auxiliary branches attached to frozen diffusion backbones, and subsequent works expanded controllability through unified multi-condition models ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ) , lightweight conditioning adapters ( Mou et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2023 ) , feedback-based control architectures ( Li et al., 2024 ; Zavadski et al., 2024 ) , grounded and regional generation ( Li et al., 2023b ; Xie et al., 2023 ; Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ) , and training-free feature manipulation ( Mo et al., 2024 ; Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) . Sketch-based conditioning has similarly progressed through dedicated sketch-to-image and interactive systems ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2024 ) toward increasingly general conditional generators. These developments largely assume a condition that is already sufficiently specified before generation begins. The transition from UNet diffusion to DiT and rectified-flow architectures ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ) has further changed how spatial conditions are injected. Ctrl-Adapter ( Lin et al., 2025 ) bridges pretrained ControlNets to newer diffusion backbones, OminiControl ( Tan et al., 2025 ) introduces lightweight universal control for FLUX, and SemanticDraw ( Lee et al., 2025 ) supports real-time multi-region interaction. ControlNet-XS ( Zavadski et al., 2024 ) and ControlNet++ ( Li et al., 2024 ) likewise revisit the interaction between the conditioning pathway and the generator. While these methods considerably expand what can be controlled, their conditioning remains predominantly generation-centric rather than progression-centric: the model receives the current condition, but does not explicitly reason about what should remain stable from the preceding interaction turn. ProgressNet instead treats the previous concept as part of the state of generation and explicitly distinguishes stroke addition, removal, and prompt reinterpretation.

sections.heading: Real-Time and Iterative Image Editing.
sections.text: Diffusion editing has been extensively studied through inversion and attention manipulation ( Hertz et al., 2023 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Couairon et al., 2023 ; Kawar et al., 2023 ; Mokady et al., 2023 ) , inpainting ( Avrahami et al., 2023 ; Lugmayr et al., 2022 ; Suvorov et al., 2022 ) , instruction-based editing ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) , and personalization ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Ruiz et al., 2023 ; Gal et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ) . Such methods enable semantic or regional modification but generally solve each edit as a fresh optimization, inversion, or generation problem rather than maintaining a persistent state across a long interaction sequence. Few-step and distilled generation substantially reduce this cost. Latent Consistency Models ( Luo et al., 2023 ) , SDXS ( Song et al., 2024 ) , NitroFusion ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , SDXL-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2023 ) , and StreamDiffusion ( Kodaira et al., 2025 ) push inference toward interactive rates. However, low latency alone does not imply temporal consistency: regenerating from a changed sketch can alter previously established identity, appearance, geometry, or background even when the newly introduced stroke is local. Among interactive sketch systems, Block-and-Detail ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ) stabilizes generation through coarse-to-fine re-noising, whereas SDXS ( Song et al., 2024 ) provides one-step image-conditioned synthesis; both remain vulnerable to drift when the conditioning evolves progressively. Recent training-free editing methods are particularly related to our temporal component. StableFlow ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) identifies vital transformer layers and reuses internal features to preserve content during editing, while FluxSpace ( Dalva et al., 2025 ) exposes semantic directions in rectified-flow representations and FLUX.1 Kontext ( Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ) enables iterative in-context editing. Related feature-reuse mechanisms have also been explored for consistency through cross-image or temporal attention ( Alaluf et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2023 ; Qi et al., 2023 ) . These works demonstrate that internal attention features provide a strong substrate for consistency, but progressive sketching requires a different balance: preserving all influential layers too strongly can suppress newly drawn structure. This motivates our Layer-Selective K/V Injection, which preserves temporal information only through non-vital layers while leaving structurally important layers free to adapt.

sections.heading: Condition Misalignment and Adaptive Control.
sections.text: A separate literature studies the failure of text and visual conditions to remain semantically aligned. Text-to-image models exhibit semantic neglect, incorrect attribute binding, and word-to-concept mismatch ( Rassin et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , with such failures analyzed through cross-attention ( Tang et al., 2023 ) and latent-space representations ( Ramos et al., 2025 ) . Structured Diffusion ( Feng et al., 2023 ) decomposes prompts for improved compositionality, while Attend-and-Excite ( Chefer et al., 2023 ) , Linguistic Binding ( Rassin et al., 2023 ) , and Attention Refocusing ( Phung et al., 2024 ) intervene on attention to improve semantic correspondence. More directly related to ProgressNet, SmartControl ( Liu et al., 2024 ) adapts ControlNet behavior under rough or unreliable visual conditions, while Text-Anchored Score Composition ( Wang et al., 2024 ) explicitly addresses conflict between textual and spatial conditions. Conditional Balance ( Cohen et al., 2025 ) controls competing conditioning signals through selective feature manipulation, and training-free alternatives such as Ctrl-X ( Lin et al., 2024 ) and FreeControl ( Mo et al., 2024 ) regulate structure and appearance without conventional task-specific training. Collectively, these methods show that a single fixed global control scale is insufficient when text and structural evidence disagree. Progressive sketching makes this conflict substantially more difficult because the disagreement itself changes over time. A sparse early contour may be highly ambiguous or even contradict the prompt, whereas later strokes can progressively resolve the intended geometry. The appropriate strength of control can therefore vary across interaction turns, architectural layers, and denoising steps. Our pilot analysis further shows that ControlNet perturbations are step- and band-asymmetric and that large inter-turn feature redistribution accompanies structurally disruptive stroke updates. ProgressNet exploits this behavior through Banded Adaptive Control (BAC), deriving step- and band-specific correction factors from retrospective comparisons of cached tile-memory ControlNet features across preceding turns. Unlike learned control policies ( Liu et al., 2024 ) or manually selected control locations ( Cohen et al., 2025 ) , BAC derives its modulation directly from the evolving control representation and requires no additional training.

sections.heading: Appendix F Nano Banana Pro
sections.text: Nano Banana Pro, a commercial image-generation and editing model by Google DeepMind, is included as a qualitative reference in Fig. 8 of the main paper. For fine-grained spatial-control comparisons, the same sketch and text instruction were supplied through its public chat interface, with an explicit request to follow the sketch structure. Because the system is proprietary and does not expose the controlled inference protocol required by our completion-level evaluation, we do not include it in the quantitative tables. The comparison is therefore intended only to illustrate differences in interactive sketch adherence under the available interface, not to establish a controlled benchmark ranking.

Image generators do not work this way. They typically take a finished sketch and produce the image in a single pass, so every edit starts the picture again, and the models that do keep state across turns are driven by text, cannot take a stroke, and are too slow to draw with. We present ProgressNet , a training-free framework that lets a frozen text-to-image model follow a drawing session as it unfolds: strokes are added and erased, the prompt is revised, and the image keeps up at about a second per turn. It needs no new parameters because the frozen model already has what a progressive generator needs, a pathway through which the previous turn can be remembered, layers that can carry appearance forward without freezing structure, and an internal signal of how far to trust an unfinished sketch; three inference-time mechanisms ( Previous-Concept Memory , Layer-Selective K/V Injection and Banded Adaptive Control ) use each in turn. As a sketch fills in, every existing method degrades, the FID of the FLUX+ControlNet baseline doubling between 10% and 100% completion on FS-COCO, while ProgressNet’s barely moves; it maintains strong fidelity and progressive coherence across three sketch domains and is preferred by users over five competitors, most widely on erasure. Figure 1: ProgressNet follows a drawing session turn by turn, training-free on frozen FLUX. Top : the cat’s body is erased and it moves onto a platform, stands once legs are drawn, loses its tail when it is erased, and walks into a river once the tail is redrawn. Bottom : a scene is built stroke by stroke, re-themed by the prompt from snowy to green, and finished with a house and birds. 1 Introduction Humans are visual creatures. We drew before we wrote, and drawing remains the most natural way to think through a visual idea and share it. Generative AI has opened a remarkable channel for this: a sentence now produces a picture ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ) , in well under a second with few-step distillation ( Luo et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2023 ) , and because a sentence is a poor description of a picture, control has steadily grown beyond text, to edges, depth and layout ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Mou et al., 2024 ) , to reference images ( Ye et al., 2023 ; Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ) , and most recently to a sketch drawn beside the prompt box ( OpenAI, 2026 ) . Sketch is the natural end of that road: it is how people convey shape and intent when words run out ( Eitz et al., 2012 ; Koley et al., 2024 ) . Yet every one of these systems takes the sketch as a finished input and produces the image in a single pass, and nobody draws that way. A drawing is made over time: a few strokes, a look, a stroke erased, a line redrawn, often a change of mind about what the picture is of ( Fig. 1 ). What a person needs is not a picture from a sketch but a picture that keeps up with the sketching: one that follows each added stroke, lets go of each erased one, absorbs a revised prompt, leaves everything else untouched, and answers fast enough to feel like a response rather than a resubmission. This paper is about that interaction. ProgressNet lets a frozen text-to-image model support all of it, drawing, erasing and prompt revision, at about a second per turn and with no training. Figure 2: Flux+ControlNet imprints raw stroke edges and visually drifts across progressive turns; ours adapts smoothly while maintaining temporal coherence. To the best of our knowledge, no existing system does all. Sketch-conditioned generation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Koley et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) is stateless: each turn regenerates the scene from nothing, so appearance drifts with every stroke and an erased stroke leaves a ghost, because nothing withdraws the evidence it added ( Fig. 2 ). Interactive sketch systems lower the cost of regeneration without removing its statelessness ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2024 ) , and Subjective Camera ( Chen et al., 2025b ) follows a drawing order by latent optimisation that takes minutes per scene. Image editing models ( Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) do handle turn-by-turn interaction, but for a different kind of turn: the image enters as a second token stream in joint attention and the change is given in words, so there is no pathway for a stroke map and no way to say that a stroke is gone, and tens of denoising steps over a doubled sequence make each turn take seconds rather than the fraction of a second a drawing person will wait. ProgressNet therefore builds on the architecture that accepts strokes, a frozen flow-matching backbone with a ControlNet, and stays in the few-step regime that makes interaction possible. Following a drawing session with a frozen model raises three problems, and each has a simple answer inside the model. Remembering. The model must remember what it generated last turn. The ControlNet’s tile branch accepts an RGB image, so the previous output can be fed back as an explicit appearance memory, and because that memory lives in pixel space the user’s operations map onto it directly: an added stroke keeps it, an erased stroke white-fills its region, a new prompt relaxes the regions the user has not committed to ( Previous-Concept Memory , PCM; Section 4.1 ). Carrying forward. The model must carry that memory without freezing what should change. Training-free editors inject cached attention at the layers most vital to forming the image ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) ; under progression those are exactly the layers that must absorb new strokes, and locking them yields images that stop responding as the drawing grows. Injecting at the least vital layers instead keeps appearance while structure stays free ( Layer-Selective K/V Injection , LS-KVI; Section 4.2 ). Trusting the sketch. The model must balance adherence to an unfinished sketch with preservation of previous appearance. We regulate this balance indirectly, using changes in cached ControlNet memory features between the two preceding completed turns to modulate memory strength across layer bands and solver steps, while structural control remains fixed (Banded Adaptive Control, BAC; Section 4.3 ). Together the three add 0.068 0.068 s to a two-step FLUX generation. The result is a generator whose quality does not decay as the drawing fills in: on FS-COCO ( Chowdhury et al., 2022 ) the FID of FLUX+ControlNet doubles between 10% and 100% completion and every baseline degrades the same way, while ProgressNet’s moves by under one point. Because frame-to-frame similarity alone rewards a method that ignores the new stroke, we introduce a progressive fidelity-coherence score (PFC) combining temporal coherence with completion-level distributional quality. Our contributions are (i) the first training-free system for progressive generation from sketch and text that supports stroke addition, erasure and prompt revision at interactive rates; (ii) PCM, LS-KVI and BAC, with the findings that vital-layer injection over-locks under progression and that inter-turn ControlNet feature redistribution is a usable online control signal, validated across two backbones and four sketch domains; (iii) a protocol and score for progressive generation, with results on three sketch domains and user study in which ProgressNet is preferred over five competitors, most widely on erasure. None of the three mechanisms is sketch-specific. 2 Related Work Controllable image generation spans ControlNet-style residual conditioning ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , multi-condition control ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , lightweight adapters ( Mou et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2023 ) , layout grounding ( Li et al., 2023b ; Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ) , and training-free feature steering ( Mo et al., 2024 ; Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) , recently ported to DiT and rectified-flow backbones ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Tan et al., 2025 ) . Inversion-based editing ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) , attention injection ( Avrahami et al., 2025 ) , and few-step distillation ( Song et al., 2024 ; Sauer et al., 2023 ) improve editability and latency, bringing sketch interaction near real time ( Sarukkai et al., 2024 ) . Others mitigate text-sketch conflict by re-weighting cross-attention ( Chefer et al., 2023 ; Phung et al., 2024 ) or rescaling the control residual ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Cohen et al., 2025 ) . All operate single-shot: none tracks how sketch–text conflict evolves across turns, nor preserves prior content as the condition changes. ProgressNet targets this non-stationary setting via training-free temporal memory, selective feature reuse, and ControlNet-driven adaptive control, detailed in Appendix E . 3 Preliminaries ProgressNet builds on flow-matching backbones ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2025 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) with Union ControlNet. Joint attention over latent and context tokens exposes the K/V features later reused by LS-KVI ( Section 4.2 ), while spatial conditions such as Canny edges and tile memory are introduced through ControlNet residuals, 𝐡 ′ = 𝐡 + λ ​ 𝐫 \mathbf{h}^{\prime}=\mathbf{h}+\lambda\mathbf{r} . This formulation also makes the control strength λ \lambda a critical factor under few-step inference, where over- or under-conditioning cannot be corrected over many denoising steps ( Section 4.3 ). Our pilot studies ( Figs. 3a and 3b ) show that existing formulations struggle to maintain a coherent progressive state: appearance can drift between turns, a fixed control strength can either imprint partial strokes too strongly or under-enforce them, and erased content may persist when the sketch is revised. ProgressNet addresses these coupled failures through explicit concept memory, selective temporal feature reuse, and adaptive control modulation. (a) Progressive sketching. (b) Stroke removal and re-addition. (a) Under progressive sketching, FLUX+ControlNet and StableFlow show temporal instability and artifacts on the partial strokes ( red borders), while ours remains stable across turns. (b) When strokes are removed and re-added (Seq. 1-3), FLUX+ControlNet fails to preserve established concepts, shifting identity across turns. 4 Proposed Methodology Overview. Progressive generation differs from text-guided editing. In editing, feature injection preserves a source image while text updates selected semantics. PCM and LS-KVI preserve temporal consistency, while BAC uses retrospective memory-feature divergence to adapt memory. ProgressNet enables progressive drawing by improving fidelity and alignment across completion levels with near-real-time performance. Our work opens avenues for more modality-agnostic progressive generation. Limitations. (i) ProgressNet is primarily evaluated with sketch-based control; extending its memory and adaptive-control mechanisms to other modalities, such as depth and pose, remains unexplored. (ii) BAC uses predefined layer bands and modulation bounds; automatically identifying control-sensitive regions on different conditioning modalities is a promising future direction.
